Main.sentence: Molokaʻi or Molokai [a] is the fifth most populated of the eight major islands that make up the ___E:Hawaiian Islands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Islands)___ archipelago in the middle of the ___E:Pacific Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean)___ .

It is 38 by 10 miles (61 by 16 km) at its greatest length and width with a usable land area of 260 sq mi (673.40 km 2 ), making it the fifth largest in size of the main Hawaiian Islands and the ___E:27th-largest island in the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_the_United_States_by_area)___ .

It lies southeast of ___E:Oʻahu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oahu)___ across the 25-mile-wide (40 km) ___E:Kaʻiwi Channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_islands_channels)___ and north of ___E:Lānaʻi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanai)___ , separated from it by the ___E:Kalohi Channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_islands_channels)___ .

The island's agrarian economy has been driven primarily by cattle ranching, ___E:pineapple U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pineapple)___ production, ___E:sugarcane U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarcane)___ production and small-scale farming.

Tourism comprises a small fraction of the island's economy, and much of the infrastructure related to tourism was closed and barricaded in the early 2000s when the primary landowner, Molokai Ranch, ceased operations due to substantial revenue losses.

In ___E:Kalawao County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalawao_County)___ , on the ___E:Kalaupapa Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalaupapa_Peninsula)___ on the north coast, settlements were established in 1866 for quarantined treatment of persons with ___E:leprosy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leprosy)___ ; these operated until 1969. The ___E:Kalaupapa National Historical Park U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalaupapa_National_Historical_Park)___ now preserves this entire county and area. Several other islands are visible from the shores of Molokaʻi, including Oʻahu from the west shores; Lānaʻi from the south shores, and ___E:Maui U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui)___ from the south and east shores.
The island is known under several names by the local population: Molokaʻi ʻĀina Momona (land of abundance), Molokaʻi Pule Oʻo (powerful prayer), and Molokaʻi Nui A Hina (of the goddess Hina).

Both the form Molokai (without an ___E:ʻokina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CA%BBokina)___ ) and Molokaʻi (with) have long been used by native speakers of Hawaiian, and there is debate as to which is the original form, with conflicting claims as to which the elders used.  The ___E:USGS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USGS)___ and the Hawaiʻi Board on Geographic Names use the form with the ʻokina.

Molokaʻi developed from two distinct ___E:shield volcanoes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shield_volcano)___ known as ___E:East Molokaʻi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Molokai_Volcano)___ and the much smaller ___E:West Molokaʻi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauna_Loa_(Molokai))___ .
The highest point is Kamakou  on East Molokaʻi, at 4,970 ft (1,510 m).

Today, East Molokaʻi volcano, like the ___E:Koʻolau Range U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koolau_Range)___ on ___E:Oʻahu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oahu)___ , is what remains of the southern half of the original mountain.

The northern half suffered a catastrophic collapse about 1.5 million years ago and now lies as a debris field scattered northward across the bottom of the ___E:Pacific Ocean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean)___ .
What remains of the volcano on the island include the highest ___E:sea cliffs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_cliff)___ in the world.
The south shore of Molokaʻi boasts the longest ___E:fringing reef U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fringing_reef)___ in the U.S. and its holdings—nearly 25 mi (40 km) long.

Molokaʻi is part of the state of ___E:Hawaii U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii)___ and located in ___E:Maui County, Hawaii U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui_County,_Hawaii)___ , except for the Kalaupapa Peninsula, which is separately administered as ___E:Kalawao County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalawao_County)___ .
Maui County encompasses Maui, ___E:Lanai U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanai)___ , and ___E:Kahoolawe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahoolawe)___ in addition to Molokaʻi.

The largest town on the island is ___E:Kaunakakai U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaunakakai,_Hawaii)___ , which is one of two small ports on the island. ___E:Molokai Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molokai_Airport)___ is located on the central plains of Molokaʻi.

The ___E:United States Census Bureau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau)___ divides the island into three ___E:census tracts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census_tract)___ , Census Tract 317 and Census Tract 318 of Maui County and Census Tract 319 of Kalawao County.
The total ___E:2010 census U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census,_2010)___ population of these was 7,345,  living on a land area of 260.02 sq mi (673.45 km 2 ).

Molokaʻi is separated from Oahu to the northwest by the ___E:Molokai Channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molokai_Channel)___ , from Maui to the southeast by the ___E:Pailolo Channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channels_of_the_Hawaiian_Islands#Pailolo_Channel)___ and from Lanai to the south by the ___E:Kalohi Channel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalohi_Channel)___ .
The Kauhako Crater Lake is a ___E:soda lake U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soda_lake)___ .
Molokaʻi is split into two main geographical areas.
The low western half is very dry and the soil is heavily denuded due to poor land management practices, which allowed over-grazing by deer and goats.
It lacks significant ground cover and virtually the entire section is covered in non-native kiawe ( Prosopis pallida ) trees.

One of the few natural areas remaining almost intact are the coastal ___E:dunes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dune)___ of ___E:Moʻomomi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moomomi&action=edit&redlink=1)___ , which are part of a ___E:Nature Conservancy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nature_Conservancy)___ preserve.

The eastern half of the island is a high ___E:plateau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau)___ rising up to an elevation of 4,900 ft (1,500 m) on Kamakou peak and includes the 2,774-acre (11.23 km 2 ; 4.334 sq mi) Molokai Forest Reserve.

The eastern half is covered with lush ___E:wet forests U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_wet_forests)___ that get more than 300 in (7,600 mm) of rain per year. The high-elevation forests are populated by native ʻōhiʻa lehua ( Metrosideros polymorpha ) trees and an extremely diverse endemic flora and fauna in the ___E:understory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Understory)___ .
Much of the summit area is protected by the Nature Conservancy's Kamakou and Pelekunu valley preserves.

Below 4,000 ft (1,200 m), the vegetation is dominated by introduced and invasive flora, including ___E:strawberry guava U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawberry_guava)___ ( Psidium littorale ), eucalyptus ( Eucalyptus spp.), and cypress ( Cupressus spp.).

Introduced ___E:axis deer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chital)___ ( Axis axis ) and ___E:feral pigs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feral_pigs)___ ( Sus scrofa ) roam native forests, destroying native plants, expanding spreading invasive plants through disturbance and distribution of their seeds, and threatening endemic ___E:insects U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insect)___ .

Near the summit of Kamakou is the unique ___E:Pēpēʻōpae U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepeopae)___ ___E:bog U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_tropical_rainforests#Bogs)___ , where dwarf ʻōhiʻa and other plants cover the soggy ground.
Molokaʻi is home to a great number of ___E:endemic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endemism)___ plant and animal species.

However, many of its species, including the olomaʻo ( Myadestes lanaiensis ), kākāwahie ( Paroreomyza flammea ), and the ___E:Bishop's ‘ō‘ō U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moho_bishopi)___ ( Moho bishopi ) have become ___E:extinct U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extinction)___ .
Molokaʻi is home to a wingless fly among many other endemic insects.

It used to be thought that Molokaʻi was first settled around AD 650 by ___E:indigenous peoples U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples)___ most likely from the ___E:Marquesas Islands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquesas_Islands)___ .

However, a 2010 study using revised, high-precision radiocarbon dating based on more reliable samples has established that the period of eastern Polynesian colonization of the Marquesas Islands took place much later, in a shorter time frame of two waves: the "earliest in the Society Islands c. 1025–1120, four centuries later than previously assumed; then after 70 to 265 years, dispersal continued in one major pulse to all remaining islands c. 1190–1290."  Later migrants likely came from ___E:Tahiti U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahiti)___ and other south Pacific islands.

Although Captain ___E:James Cook U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook)___ recorded sighting Molokaʻi in 1778, the first European sailor to visit the island was ___E:Captain George Dixon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Dixon_(Royal_Navy_officer))___ of the British Royal Navy in 1786.  The first significant European influence came in 1832 when a Protestant mission was established at Kaluaʻaha on the East End of the island by the ___E:Reverend Harvey Hitchcock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Rexford_Hitchcock)___ .

The first farmer on Molokaʻi to grow, produce and mill sugar and coffee commercially was ___E:Rudolph Wilhelm Meyer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph_Wilhelm_Meyer)___ , an immigrant from Germany who arrived in 1850. He built the first and only ___E:sugar mill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarcane_mill)___ on the island in 1878, which is now a museum.

Ranching began on Molokaʻi in the first half of the 19th century when ___E:King Kamehameha V U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamehameha_V)___ set up a country estate on the island, which was managed by Meyer and became what is now the Molokai Ranch.

In the late 1800s, Kamehameha V built a vacation home in ___E:Kaunakakai U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaunakakai)___ and ordered the planting of over 1,000 coconut trees in Kapuaiwa Coconut Grove.

___E:Leprosy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leprosy)___ (also known as Hansen's disease) was introduced to the Hawaiian Islands by traders, sailors, workers and others who lived in societies where it was ___E:endemic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endemic)___ .
Sugar planters were worried about the effects on their labor force and pressured the government to take action to control the spread of leprosy.
The legislature passed a control act requiring quarantine of people with leprosy.

The government established ___E:Kalawao U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalawao)___ located on the isolated Kalaupapa peninsula on the northern side of Molokaʻi, followed by ___E:Kalaupapa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalaupapa)___ as the sites of a leper colony that operated from 1866 to 1969. Because Kalaupapa had a better climate and sea access, it developed as the main community.
A research hospital was developed at Kalawao.
The population of these settlements reached a peak of 1,100 shortly after the beginning of the 20th century.

In total over the decades, more than 8,500 men, women and children living throughout the Hawaiian islands and diagnosed with leprosy were exiled to the colony by the Hawaiian government and declared ___E:legally dead U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_death)___ .
This public health measure was continued after the Kingdom became a U.S. territory.
Patients were not allowed to leave the settlement nor have visitors and had to live out their days here.
___E:Arthur Albert St. Mouritz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Albert_St._Mouritz)___ served as a physician to the leper settlement from 1884 to 1887.    He explained how leprosy was spread.

___E:Pater Damiaan de Veuster U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pater_Damiaan)___ (Father Damien), a ___E:Belgian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium)___ ___E:priest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priesthood_(Catholic_Church))___ of the ___E:Congregation of the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_of_the_Sacred_Hearts_of_Jesus_and_Mary)___ served as a missionary for 16 years in the communities of sufferers of leprosy. ___E:Joseph Dutton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Dutton)___ , who served in the 13th Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry Regiment during the ___E:American Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War)___ and converted to ___E:Roman Catholicism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholicism)___ in 1883, came to Molokaʻi in 1886 to help Father Damien and the rest of the population who suffered from leprosy.

Father Damien died at Kalaupapa in 1889 while Joseph Dutton died in Honolulu in 1931 at the age of 87. ___E:Mother Marianne Cope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_Marianne_Cope)___ of the ___E:Sisters of Saint Francis of Syracuse, New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Order_of_St._Francis#Sisters_of_St._Francis_of_Philadelphia)___ , brought six of her Sisters to work in Hawaiʻi with leprosy sufferers in the late 19th century, also serving on Molokaʻi.

Both Father Damien and Mother Marianne have been ___E:canonized as Saints by the Roman Catholic Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonization)___ for their charitable work and devotion to sufferers of leprosy.
In December 2015, the cause of Joseph Dutton was formally opened, obtaining him the title ___E:Servant of God U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servant_of_God)___ .

In the 1920s, people confined in the leper colony were treated with a new method devised by ___E:Alice Ball U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Ball)___ and involving ___E:chaulmoogra oil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydnocarpus_wightianus#Leprosy)___ .
In the 1940s, ___E:sulfonamide drugs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfonamide_(medicine))___ were developed and provided a more effective treatment.

Antibiotic ___E:Dapsone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dapsone)___ has been used for leprosy since 1945.  Modern Multidrug therapy (MDT) remains highly effective, and people are no longer infectious after the first monthly dose.
In 1969, the century-old laws of forced quarantine were abolished.
Former patients living in Kalaupapa today have chosen to remain here, most for the rest of their lives.

In the 21st century, there are no persons on the island with active cases of leprosy, which has been controlled through medication, but some former patients chose to continue to live in the settlement after its official closure.

Over the years ___E:Molokai Ranch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Molokai_Ranch&action=edit&redlink=1)___ has also acted as a developer, establishing hotels and related amenities for resort tourists on their property.

The local indigenous community fought for many decades to inhibit the development by Molokai Ranch in order to preserve their community and unique way of life. In some cases, protests have become violent, such as fence cutting, poisoning of the Ranch's exotic African Safari animals in 1994, an arson attack in Kaupoa in 1995, and the destruction of 5 mi (8 km) of Ranch water pipes in 1996.
In 2007, community residents organized the "Save Laʻau Point" movement to oppose Molokai Ranch's attempt to expand its resort operation.

As a result, on March 24, 2008, Molokai Ranch, then the island's largest employer, decided to shut down all resort operations, including hotels, movie theater, restaurants, and golf course, and dismiss 120 workers.

In September 2017 the company that owns Molokai Ranch, ___E:Singapore U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore)___ -based Guoco Leisure Ltd, put this 55,575-acre (22,490 ha) property, encompassing 35% of the island of Molokaʻi, on the market for $260 million.

After years of neglect, residents have ___E:organized U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_organizing)___ and formed the Molokai Heritage Trust to determine how to eventually buy back the land, return it to the stewardship of the local community, and protect it from exploitation.
Due to the fight against development and tourism, Molokaʻi has Hawaii's highest unemployment rate. The residents have fought hard to maintain a lifestyle based on indigenous subsistence practices.

This lifestyle is not without challenges, however, and many live below the federal poverty line. One third of its residents use ___E:food stamps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplemental_Nutrition_Assistance_Program)___ .

As of 2014 [update] , the largest industry on the island is seed production for ___E:Monsanto U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsanto)___ and ___E:Mycogen Seeds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycogen_Seeds)___ , including ___E:GMO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GMO)___ seeds.
The tourism industry on Molokaʻi is relatively small, compared to the other islands in Hawaiʻi.

Only 64,767 tourists visited Molokaʻi in 2015.  For decades, residents of Molokaʻi have resisted private developers' attempts to increase tourism because of the irreparable changes to community and culture that are associated with a tourism industry.
Accommodations are limited; as of 2014, only one hotel was open on the island.
Most tourists find lodgings at rental condos and houses.

National Geographic Traveler magazine and the National Geographic Center for Sustainable Destinations conduct annual Destination Scorecard surveys, aided by ___E:George Washington University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_University)___ .

In 2007, a panel of 522 experts in ___E:sustainable tourism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_tourism)___ and destination stewardship reviewed 111 selected human-inhabited ___E:islands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island)___ and ___E:archipelagos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archipelago)___ around the world.
Molokaʻi ranked 10th among the 111 destination locales.
The survey cited Molokaʻi's undeveloped tropical landscape, environmental stewardship, and rich, deep Hawaiian traditions (the island's mana ).

The neighbor islands of ___E:Hawaiʻi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_(island))___ , ___E:Kauaʻi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaua%CA%BBi)___ , ___E:Maui U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui)___ and ___E:Oʻahu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%CA%BBahu)___ , ranked 50, 61, 81 and 104, respectively.
Molokaʻi is believed to be the birthplace of the ___E:hula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hula)___ .
The annual ___E:Molokaʻi Ka Hula Piko U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moloka%CA%BBi_Ka_Hula_Piko)___ festival is held on this island.
Molokaʻi can be reached by plane.

Planes fly into Molokaʻi daily from other Hawaiian islands including Oʻahu (Honolulu and Kalaeloa), Maui (Kahului) and Hawaii (Kona), operated by ___E:Mokulele Airlines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mokulele_Airlines)___ , Paragon Air and ___E:Hawaiian Airlines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Airlines)___ .

A ferry that formerly sailed between Molokaʻi and ___E:Lāhainā U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C4%81hain%C4%81)___ Harbor, Maui closed operations on October 27, 2016. Sea Link President and Senior Capt. Dave Jung attributed the closure to competition from federally subsidized commuter air travel and declining ridership.
The island of Molokaʻi is served by Molokaʻi General Hospital, which operates all day, every day. It is also serviced by Molokai Community Health Center.
All areas of the state of Hawaii are in one school district: ___E:Hawaii State Department of Education U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_State_Department_of_Education)___ .

The island public school system includes four elementary schools, one charter school, one middle school, and one high school, ___E:Molokaʻi High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moloka%CA%BBi_High_School)___ .
There is also a community college.
The island has one private middle/high school.
The ___E:Hawaii State Public Library System U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_State_Public_Library_System)___ operates the Molokai Public Library in Kaunakakai.
The island contains many parks and other protected areas, but most parks do not have service staff, potable water, or restroom facilities.

Parks within the Maui County parks jurisdiction include Palaʻau State Park, Kiowea Beach Park, Kakahaiʻa National Wildlife Refuge, Molokaʻi Forest Reserve, Pelekunu Preserve, George Murphy Beach Park, Hālawa Beach Park, and Papohaku Beach Park (with a 2 mi [3.2 km] beach) in the portion within Maui County.

Today Kalawao County is preserved by the ___E:Kalaupapa National Historical Park U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalaupapa_National_Historical_Park)___ (accessible by guided ___E:mule U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mule)___ or hiking tour).

The island can be traversed by a two-lane highway running east to west: Highway 460 (Maunaloa Highway) from the west side town of Maunaloa to Kaunakakai, and Highway 450 (King Kamehameha V Highway) from Kaunakakai to the Hālawa Beach Park. Highway 470 is a spur up to the barrier mountains of Kalawao County and the Kalaupapa peninsula.
By land this area (Kalaupapa) can only be reached by a hiking trail.
Mule rides on the trail were suspended in 2018 when the trail temporarily closed due to a landslide and bridge damage.
Most access to the Kalaupapa peninsula is by sea.
Maui Economic Opportunity operates public transportation on Molokaʻi.
